newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Eating gets cheaper under Islamist Afghan rulers.
newsitem.headline: Eating gets cheaper under Islamist Afghan rulers.

text.p: While many people in Kabul grumble about, and even fear, their new puritan Islamist rulers, many small traders and truckers said on Thursday they were delighted the old government had been ousted.
"Before you had to hide your money well because you never knew when the mujahideen would come looting and business was awful," said a foreign currency dealer in the Afghan capital.
"But the Taleban are very disciplined, there's no stealing, everything is safe and business is smooth."

The Taleban militia, their movement born in religious schools in refugee camps in Pakistan two years ago, took Kabul a week ago and immediately started imposing a purist brand of Islam, telling women to stay home and men to grow beards.

Afghanistan -- the Taleban now control about three-quarters of it -- would be ruled by Islamic law, with thieves punished by amputation and adulterers stoned to death, the Taleban's high council decreed.

The decree has frightened many educated people in Kabul, Afghanistan's most liberal city, where a communist government that fell in 1992 had encouraged women's education and where Western dress for both sexes was common.
Now many people are trying to leave the city of one million that has known only war, destruction and fear since mujahideen guerrillas took over in 1992.

But small traders said on Thursday that life had improved dramatically for them since the Taleban entered the city because trade was back to something approaching normal and prices had dropped sharply.
The U.S. dollar, worth 21,000 afghanis before the Taleban arrived, was changing hands at 15,000 on Thursday.
The Pakistani rupee, a critical currency because so many of Kabul's staples come from Pakistan, was worth about 300 afghanis on Thursday compared to 500 a week ago.
The re-opening of the road over the Khyber Pass, even though it is in an extremely rough state for much of its length, means more regular supplies.
The departure of the old government has also added to supplies because it used to buy food for its soldiers in the bazaar, traders said.
"That left little in the market for ordinary people, anyway, but the Taleban supply their own people themselves and that means there is a lot more in the market for ordinary people to buy," said one.
"We're very happy they're here because prices are coming down every day and people can live better," said butcher Abdul Qayyum, 50.

He was considerably less happy about the price the Taleban had imposed on mutton, a Kabul staple. Qayyum said the Taleban arrived at the central market where he has his small stall and told butchers the price of mutton was 15,000 afghanis a kg, compared to 21,000 in neighbouring provinces.

"This is not a good price because the cost of sheep is very high and I'm not making much money. Nobody's been to check on us, but we're afraid of what might happen to us if we don't sell at the set price," he said. "But it does mean ordinary people can afford to eat a little meat again."
Before the Taleban took Kabul, eating in the capital was a problem. A school teacher, for instance, earns about 70,000 Afghanis a month -- not enough to feed a family, Kabulis say.

The flour for Afghanistan's staple naan, an unleavened bread, cost 32,000 afghanis for seven kg (15.5 lbs). Mutton was 22,000 a kg (2.2 lbs), onions 10,000 and potatoes 18,000. The average family would use seven kg of firewood to cook its food a day, costing up to 9,000 afghanis.
On Thursday, the seven kg of flour cost 19,500 afghanis, onions 8,000, potatoes 15,000 and firewood 5,000.
A group of truckers who had just brought a load of firewood from Paktia province south of Kabul said they were delighted the old government had gone.

"It used to take us two days and two nights to bring a load to Kabul when the mujahideen were in power. They had checkpoints every few kilometres and at every one they would demand 'taxes', or take a little wood," said one.

"By the time we got to Kabul, these guys had added two million afghanis to the price of our load, which we had to pass on to our customers. Now, it takes us 11 hours to drive to Kabul, it's completely safe and nobody bothers us," he said.
"The Taleban are extremely good," he added to a chorus of approval from his friends.
